title: Virtual Environments, pip and the .env File: Why Every Project Gets Its Own

scenes.title: One laptop, two projects, one clash
scenes.body: Project A was built with **library v1**. Project B needs **library v2**. Without isolation, Python keeps **one copy** of each library for the whole computer: installing v2 for B silently breaks A. This is where "but it works on my machine!" comes from.

items.text: Projects need different versions of the same package
A global install changes every project at once
Your teammate's computer has different versions than yours

scenes.title: A virtual environment is each project's own toolbox
scenes.body: Two carpenters sharing one toolbox keep swapping each other's tools. Give each one **their own box**, and nobody's work breaks. `.venv` is that box: its own Python, its own `pip`, its own packages, inside the project folder.

scenes.heading: Activate it: one command per shell

items.text: It puts `.venv/bin` at the **front of PATH**
items.sub: remember Lesson 1: the shell searches PATH in order

items.text: So `python` and `pip` now mean the project's own copies
It changes only **this** terminal window
items.sub: a new window starts un-activated: activate again

items.text: You can skip it: `.venv/bin/python app.py` uses the venv directly
items.sub: handy in scripts and scheduled jobs

scenes.title: pip is the app store for Python
scenes.body: **PyPI** (pypi.org) is the store: hundreds of thousands of packages. **pip** is the app that downloads and installs them, into the active environment. `pip install name==version` = "install exactly this version".

scenes.body: You share a **recipe**, not a plate of food. `requirements.txt` is tiny and goes into git. `.venv` is big, machine-specific and disposable: delete it any time and cook it again from the recipe.

scenes.label: Good to know
scenes.title: `python -m pip`, and a faster tool called uv
scenes.body: `python -m pip install ...` runs the pip that belongs to **that exact Python**: the safest form when several Pythons are installed. **uv** is a newer, much faster tool that does venv + pip in one; Module 7 uses it. Learn pip first: every tool builds on the same ideas.

scenes.title: Settings belong outside the code
scenes.body: Your ATM PIN is not printed on your card. In the same way, **settings that change per machine** (debug mode, a database address) and **secrets** (API keys) don't belong in your code. The code reads them from the **environment** when it runs.

scenes.title: If a key ever leaks
scenes.body: If a real key lands in git, a chat, a screenshot or a video: **revoke it immediately** in the provider's console and create a new one. Deleting the file afterwards is not enough: copies already exist.

items.q: Why do Python projects use virtual environments?
items.a: To **isolate** each project's packages and versions, so projects don't break each other, and so the setup can be **reproduced** exactly from `requirements.txt` on any machine.
items.trap: "To make Python faster." A venv changes which packages are used, not speed.

items.a: No. Commit `requirements.txt` (the recipe) and ignore `.venv` (it is big, machine-specific and rebuildable with `pip install -r requirements.txt`).
items.trap: Committing `.venv` "so teammates don't need to install". It breaks on other operating systems and Python versions.

items.q: How do you handle API keys in a Python project?
items.a: Read them from **environment variables**, loaded from a git-ignored `.env` in development or a secrets manager in production. Commit only `.env.example` with names and placeholders. Never print or log the value; revoke a key if it leaks.
items.trap: Hard-coding the key "just for now". It ends up in git history.

scenes.question: Which file should you commit so a teammate can rebuild your environment?
scenes.explain: `requirements.txt` is the recipe. `.venv` is rebuilt from it, `.env` holds private values, and `__pycache__` is generated.

scenes.question: `os.environ.get("DEBUG")` returns `"False"`. What is `bool("False")`?
scenes.explain: Any non-empty string is truthy. Compare the text instead: `value.lower() == "true"`, as `show_config.py` does.

items.text: `.venv` = each project's own Python and packages
`python3 -m venv .venv` → `source .venv/bin/activate` → `deactivate`
`pip install pkg==x.y.z` · `pip freeze > requirements.txt` · `pip install -r`
Settings and secrets: environment variables, loaded from `.env`
Commit `.env.example`, never `.env`; revoke a key that leaks
